text: Two people are left in a Hong Kong apartment while the rest of the family sorts out Canada: a fifteen-year-old girl and her grandmother. Into that suspended household wanders Tokio, a Japanese tourist with time on his hands and no particular reason to be anywhere. Clara Law builds the comedy out of the mismatch, three people with no shared habits and no common language of daily life, thrown together in a city that is already half packed. The 108 minutes go to small transactions rather than farewells. What stands to be lost is not the family's departure, which is settled, but whatever a girl of fifteen might have learned to want from a place she is being removed from before she is old enough to argue about it. It carries a Golden Leopard.

The house has been empty for years, and Beto keeps it anyway, maintaining rooms nobody enters in a city he no longer walks into. He worked there as a domestic when the family still lived in it; the job outlasted the household. Enrique Rivero gives this eighty-two minutes, which is short for a life this narrow and exactly the right length for it: routine at the speed routine actually moves, without the pity a longer treatment would invite. Two people still reach him, the owner he obeys out of gratitude and Lupe, who is friend and lover both. Then the house is sold. What the film sets in front of Beto is not freedom but exposure, and it declines to assume he is wrong about how dangerous the street is.

A new graduate stands on a train platform and simply stops working, not a breakdown with a cause but a shutdown, the whole decade arriving at once. What puts him there is a run of images the film treats as common property: war, assassination, injustice, protest. Aram Avakian made it in 1970, close enough to those years that they are not yet history but weather. The 110 minutes that follow belong to Jacob's treatment, and the treatment is where the comedy gets in, an American picture willing to propose that the apparatus assembled to repair a young man runs on a logic no steadier than his paralysis. Nothing here holds one tone long enough to be trusted, which is either the method or the diagnosis.

Everyone in the building is asleep, and the building is coming down. István Szabó gives the night to the tenants' dreaming rather than to the wrecking ball, and what surfaces is a set of private memories that happen to contain a Hungarian century: pre-war prejudice, occupying Nazis, Stalinist scarcity. The demolition is the smaller event. Ninety-seven minutes arranged by association instead of chronology, so that a moment of sensuality can sit directly against a catastrophe with nothing between them to soften the contact. What the film asks for is patience with simultaneity, many lives and one hot night and no narrator sorting them into order. What it returns is the texture of things remembered by people who never planned to remember them.

Boredom is difficult to film without transmitting it, and Li Hongqi spends ninety-one minutes on the problem. Four teenagers pass the last day of a winter holiday at a friend's house in a northern Chinese village: talk that circles, arguments picked because an argument is something to do. Any humour has to come from timing rather than incident, since incident is precisely what the place withholds. One of them works out with his girlfriend whether being in love now will cost them later at school; another puts the whole institution on trial in a couple of flat sentences. Children reasoning like exhausted adults. Tomorrow the holiday ends and school resumes, and the fact that the prospect carries no dread at all says more than dread would.

A water jar in a village schoolyard springs a leak, and eighty-six minutes of Iranian film follow from it. The scale is exact rather than symbolic: one jar in the shade of one tree, and a school of children with nowhere else to drink. Ebrahim Forouzesh stays with the errand, who can be asked, what it costs, which adult will take responsibility for a thing everyone uses and nobody owns. A replacement cannot be had, so the problem becomes repair, and repair requires a village to agree about something. Work at this scale exposes how a community distributes obligation faster than a film about a catastrophe would, because a catastrophe hands people an excuse. A leak does not. It carries a Golden Leopard.

The man losing his faith here is not a dissident; he is a believer whose colleagues have quietly stopped bothering. Evald Schorm made it in Czechoslovakia in 1966 and put his sympathy in an awkward place, with a committed communist worker whose sincerity has become an embarrassment to everyone standing near him. The antagonist is not a person but a general slackening, the hardest thing to dramatize and the most uncomfortable to sit through, since it cannot be argued with. Eighty-five minutes. What stands to be lost is not a career but the coherence of a life organised around instructions that were meant seriously and that everyone nearby has begun to treat as optional. It holds a Golden Leopard and a Golden Kingfisher for best feature.

The older sister is certain from the moment he arrives that the man will bring disaster; she is a child, and children are not consulted. Fifteen years after leaving, he has come back to the family, and five-year-old Aurelie takes to him at once, the two girls reading the same stranger to opposite conclusions while the adults, busy with the reunion, read nothing at all. Hélène Angel films it as a thriller in an unusual sense: the dread is distributed unevenly through a household, and the people holding the authority are the ones least equipped to register it. A hundred minutes at family scale. Childhood here is not innocence but a separate country with its own intelligence, which is why the girl's suspicion outweighs every adult judgment in the picture.

The drowned woman is found first, and then the film goes looking for the living. Two couples, each inside a private crisis, move through the small hours of one British night in 1965, tied to her by nothing either of them knows about. Anthony Simmons works entirely at the hour when a city has emptied of purpose and the people still awake are the ones who cannot stop talking or cannot start. The death is a frame, not a case. That leaves ninety-four minutes resting entirely on the talk, on how two relationships sound once there is no longer anybody around to perform for. Being awake at four in the morning is a condition with its own rules, and the film is patient enough to let those rules do the work.

The father of the murdered girl and the mother of the boy who killed her end up in the same small Hokkaido town, by accident. Masahiro Kobayashi refuses to run that coincidence as a plot engine; it is a condition, to be endured across a hundred and two minutes. Both have left the places where they were known. Neither has any standing to speak to the other, and the film's interest lies in what two people do with days that still have to be filled, the work, the meals, the distance between them measured in ordinary hours. Nothing is arranged to produce forgiveness and nothing is arranged to withhold it. What gets staged is proximity, which is harder to survive than confrontation, and which films about this kind of loss usually hurry past on the way to a reckoning.

Mezz, Aziz, Laurent, Nordine and Poisson grew up in the same Parisian suburb, and Thomas Gilou's film is an accounting of what that leaves them. Garges-les-Gonesses, 1995: unemployment as weather, drugs and violence as logistics rather than events, an exit that survives mostly as a rumour. Eighty-nine minutes and a Golden Leopard, with a group in the lead instead of a hero, which lets a single afternoon cost one of them nothing and another everything. The street is not presented as a subject to be explained; it is the ground the characters stand on, and the film assumes five names can be held at once without assistance. Consolation would have to take the form of one escape, and one escape settles nothing about the others.

The threat here is not violence on screen but a list: who is on the next transport, and who has the pen. Zbyněk Brynych filmed it in Czechoslovakia in 1963, from Arnost Lustig's novel Night and Hope, and built it as a series of separate stories rather than one arc, which is the shape of a place where people are removed before their stories finish. Ninety-four minutes inside the Terezin ghetto, where ordinary business continues under an administration able to end anyone by paperwork. The visual register is dark in the plain sense as well as the figurative one. Suspense is not the mechanism, since the outcome was settled long before the camera arrived; the film spends itself on the days before, and on hope as something the residents have to keep manufacturing.

The wife's answer is no, and that refusal is the machine the whole film runs on. Mr. Zhao is a Shanghai doctor in 1998 with a wife, a mistress named Tian Jing who has just announced a pregnancy, and no aptitude whatever for the arithmetic in front of him. Lü Yue keeps to eighty-nine minutes and stays close, letting the humiliation accumulate until everyone in the arrangement can see the man clearly except the man. What holds the film upright is that the two women are not written as positions in his problem. One has a decision to make and is making it. The other made hers already, and declining to grant a divorce is neither weakness nor forgiveness but a way of holding ground that he has no instrument to measure.

A widower's method for reaching his school-age son includes getting drunk with him. Ma Lisheng is a minor party functionary by day and, at home, a man with no method at all, courting the boy's friendship one hour and shouting him down the next. Wang Shuo keeps it to ninety-six minutes at domestic scale, with no crisis imported from outside: two people negotiating an authority neither of them believes in. The son's countermove is household strategy of a high order, find the father a wife and the pressure will land somewhere else, and the candidate he settles on is the mother of a friend from school. China in 2000, a household of two, and a father whose public standing supplies him with nothing usable at his own table.
